search_bias: evaluation/verifiers; harmful/non-improving boundary; asymmetric false-commit cost; minimax regret versus alpha/error-budget design

setup.policy_library: 182 hard-deadline Bellman design pairs spanning q_low .58-.84 and q_high .58-.82 on the same 650-wealth/141-action discretization used for the predecessor T=50 comparisons.

deployment_regret_definition.good_map_regret: V*_m - Power_m(policy), where V*_m is the map-specific T=50 hard-deadline optimum.
deployment_regret_definition.non_improving_regret: kappa * Power_null_boundary(policy), treating the oracle action for q=.5 as no commit and kappa as the relative harmful/false-commit cost.
deployment_regret_definition.optimization: Choose an ex-ante policy mixture minimizing the maximum of the three good-map regrets and the non-improving regret. This keeps missed useful commits and false commits in the same explicit loss instead of calling one generic notion of robustness.

strong_harm_q04.result: For kappa up to 10 the q=.4 harmful map was non-binding: the same good-map minimax-regret mixture remained optimal because harmful crossing was already very small. At kappa=20 it became binding and selected a substantially different aggressive design near (.78,.78).
strong_harm_q04.interpretation: A clearly harmful alternative can be easier for an e-process to avoid than a boundary-null candidate; worst deployment risk can sit near q=.5 rather than at a strongly negative effect.

boundary_q05.interpretation: Once a boundary false commit is valued at roughly twice a unit of missed-oracle power, the least-favorable loss shifts and the policy sacrifices inverted-map resolution to lower realized null crossing. At larger kappa the library optimum becomes dominated by the smallest attainable boundary size rather than by useful-map balance.

alpha_separation_rule.observation: The boundary-null crossing probabilities differ by only about 0.003 absolute across the entire policy library, while good-map powers vary much more. For high kappa, using alternative-target bet shape to buy a few basis points of realized size can badly distort which useful alternatives are resolved.
alpha_separation_rule.candidate_rule: Treat the global harmful/false-commit budget alpha (or a confirmation-stage alpha allocation) as a first-class design variable separate from the alternative-side bet/power allocation. First choose an acceptable worst-case false-commit budget under the null; then optimize power/regret subject to that error budget, rather than indirectly seeking lower realized size through a mismatched alternative target.
alpha_separation_rule.scope_guard: A smaller alpha is not free; it raises the rejection threshold and can reduce all good-map power. This checkpoint has not yet computed the alpha/power Pareto frontier, so the rule is a design hypothesis supported by the observed distortion, not a completed optimization result.

new_or_updated_candidate_findings.mechanism: When assigning asymmetric harmful-commit cost, include a near-boundary q=.5 non-improving state in evaluator stress tests. Do not infer harmful safety from performance only on clearly negative q<<.5 alternatives.
new_or_updated_candidate_findings.evidence: At T=50 q=.4 rejection was only .0051-.0083 across the policy library, while q=.5 boundary rejection was .0440-.0470 and became the binding loss as kappa increased.
new_or_updated_candidate_findings.scope_guard: The exact boundary depends on the null definition; other failure modes can be harmful without mapping to paired-sign q=.5.

new_or_updated_candidate_findings.mechanism: Separate type-I/harmful-commit budget selection from alternative-side bet allocation. If false commits are much more costly, tighten or split alpha explicitly, then optimize deadline power/regret under that fixed safety budget instead of distorting the alternative target merely to exploit conservative realized size.
new_or_updated_candidate_findings.evidence: In the T=50 library, increasing boundary false-commit cost from kappa=1 to 3 moved the minimax-regret design from balanced .70/.70-.72/.70 to .72/.82, sacrificing inverted power to exploit a null-crossing reduction of only about six ten-thousandths relative to the former mixture.
new_or_updated_candidate_findings.scope_guard: Requires direct alpha/Pareto analysis before deployment; this is not evidence that one universal smaller alpha is optimal.

rejected_or_narrowed_generalizations: Rejected: 'the most harmful negative-effect map is automatically the least-favorable safety case.' A strong q=.4 alternative had much smaller false-rejection probability than the q=.5 boundary in the tested e-process family.
Rejected: 'adding a harmful map to minimax regret only changes a scalar weight, not the preferred evaluator.' At kappa>=2 the boundary-null loss changed the active policy set materially.

Narrowed: 'choose a more conservative bet when harmful commits are expensive.' Aggressive/mismatched bets can actually have lower null crossing by losing wealth faster; bet aggressiveness is not a monotone safety knob. The explicit error threshold is the interpretable safety control.

Narrowed: 'all alpha-valid policies are equivalent for harmful-commit utility.' They share a worst-case bound but can have different realized boundary size and very different good-map power, so deployment utility still requires calibration.

frontier.action: Compute the explicit alpha/power Pareto frontier at T=50/T=100 for alpha in roughly .01-.10. For each alpha, re-optimize structured fixed-latent maximin power and minimax regret including the q=.5 boundary, rather than holding the threshold at 20.
Add a confirmation-stage design with separate alpha spending for proposal and fresh audit, and compare harmful-commit utility against one-stage threshold tightening.
Stress non-sign harms where q=.5 is not the relevant boundary, including severe rare failures hidden by average paired success; keep exact tested scope.
Resume filtration-provenance and reused-development PACE path selection after the safety-budget frontier is quantified.

exact_next_action: Re-solve the T=50 structured policy game at several alpha thresholds, include q=.5 false-commit regret explicitly, and produce a Pareto table of worst good-map resolution versus worst boundary false-commit risk so alpha selection is no longer confounded with bet-shape selection.
